## Upgrading from v0.5.0

**`lift` takes `-r/--ir` in place of `-l/--lifter-type`, and names a representation rather than a tool.** `-l ghidra` becomes `-r ghidra-pcode`. There are five values now — `ghidra-pcode`, `binary-ninja-llil` / `-mlil` / `-hlil` and `ida-microcode` — and all of them are implemented.

`Error::UnsupportedIr` and `Ir::readable` are gone with the last unreadable representation. They reported which representations a build could read, and every one can be read now.

Nothing about the file format changed. A program lifted by v0.5.0 carries `"ir": "ghidra-pcode"` and reads exactly as it did.

`LifterType` is gone from the library's public API, and `LifterBuilder::new` takes an `Ir`. `AnyProgram` has gained three variants, so a `match` over it in downstream code needs three more arms.

angr is gone from that list as well. It never lifted anything — it parsed, and then reported that the angr lifter was not implemented — so the only scripts it can break are ones that were already failing.

## Highlights

- **IDA Pro lifts, to the Hex-Rays microcode.** `-r ida-microcode`, read at `MMAT_LVARS`, the last of the decompiler's maturities.

  The earlier maturities are not offered. They look like a parallel to Binary Ninja's three levels and are not: LLIL, MLIL and HLIL are representations Binary Ninja publishes, while the maturities are where a plugin may intervene in the decompiler's pipeline — the same enum holds `MMAT_ZERO`, "microcode does not exist". Nothing says their shape is stable across releases, and a representation name is permanent. On one binary four of the eight produced the same operations anyway.

  It runs through `idat`, so nothing touches your Python installation — `idalib` would have required rewriting it.

  **Producing microcode runs the decompiler, and a cloud decompiler sends each function to Hex-Rays' servers.** `lift` warns before it starts, and only when the installation has no local decompiler to use: a decompiler plugin is named `hex<arch>` locally and `hexc<arch>` when it calls out, and the API cannot be asked. It does not prompt — that would hang a script — and does not refuse, since asking for the representation is the consent. A local licence is not told its functions are being uploaded.

- **Binary Ninja lifts, to all three of its intermediate languages.** `-r binary-ninja-llil`, `-mlil` or `-hlil`. Which one answers a question is not something a tool should decide, so all three are offered and none is recommended; they are different vocabularies rather than different amounts of one, and birthmarks are not compared across them.

  It runs through `bnpython3`, Binary Ninja's own interpreter, which has the API importable already, so nothing touches your `python3` or `PYTHONPATH`. `BINARY_NINJA_HOME`, `--home`, and the usual install locations work as they do for Ghidra.

  The symbol table each file carries is keyed by whatever its level renders a call target as: an address at LLIL and MLIL, the callee's own name at HLIL, which has already resolved it.

  Binary Ninja is licensed and cannot be installed on a CI runner, so nothing in CI lifts with it. Its script is parsed on every push, and fixtures under `testdata/lifted/bnil_*/` are read back — including an assertion that each level finds the call that is in them, since a reader recognising none of its own call operations would report unrelated programs as identical.

- **The representation is the only thing you name.** `lift` used to take both a tool and, in the plan for Binary Ninja, a level within it — two arguments that could contradict each other, so something would have had to check for a combination that only existed because there were two of them. There is one now, and `-l ghidra --il hlil` cannot be written down.

  A representation implies its tool; a tool does not imply a representation, since Binary Ninja has three. Keeping the tool as the argument would have kept the one that cannot answer the question being asked — which reader can read this file, and may these two birthmarks be compared.

  Binary Ninja's three levels were declared by that change before anything lifted to them, the way `ida-microcode` still is; the entry above is what filled them in.

- **An `fc-*` birthmark that would be empty is refused, not returned.** `extract` already refused a program in which nothing is a call, because two empty birthmarks score as a perfect match and unrelated programs would come back identical. It did not refuse one whose calls all resolve to nothing, which empties the family just as thoroughly and was the way two lifters reached it during this release: the Hex-Rays microcode renders a global as `$name` and the table was keyed by the resolved name, and Binary Ninja's HLIL resolves the callee before oinkie sees it. Neither made a sound.

  It affects Ghidra too — a program whose calls are all indirect has been producing an empty `fc-*` family silently.

  The new refusal is its own error rather than the existing one, because the two send the reader to different places: nothing being a call is `is_call`, nothing resolving is the symbol table.

- **Internal links are checked on every push.** `cli/mcp/README.md` pointed at `lifter/README.md` for the whole of v0.5.0, after #91 moved that directory, and nothing noticed. There are 32 internal links now, across three kinds of README and the site.

  It is a script rather than an off-the-shelf checker because the repository holds two kinds of link that do not resolve the same way. A README's `assets/lifters/ghidra/README.md` is a path on disk; the site's `../run` is the URL `/usage/run`, whose file is `usage/run.md`. A filesystem checker reports every site link as broken.

  It reads Markdown and looks at the filesystem — no network, no build — so it costs seconds. Code regions are not scanned: link-shaped text inside a fenced example is not a link, and these READMEs are mostly examples. Reference-style links are, because a check that only saw one syntax could be bypassed by choosing the other.

  External links are checked weekly instead, opening an issue rather than failing a push — someone else's site being down for ten minutes is not a reason to fail a build — and updating that issue rather than opening another one every Monday.

- **oinkie is ready to go to crates.io, as a library and as a binary.** The manifest had four keys and none of them a licence, which crates.io refuses an upload without — the `LICENSE` file has been here since the first commit and the manifest had never said so.

  It also had no `exclude`, so the crate carried 100 files and 2.2 MB, most of it `testdata/`, the Hugo site and the workflows. It carries 62 files and 690 KiB now.

  Written as exclusions rather than as an `include` whitelist on purpose: three lifting scripts are compiled in with `include_str!`, and a whitelist that forgot the next one would build here and fail for whoever ran `cargo add`. `tests/package_test.rs` asserts that no `exclude` rule covers a compiled-in file, and that its own list has not fallen behind the `include_str!` calls in `src/`.

  `AnyProgram` derives `Debug`, without which `unwrap_err` does not compile — found by writing the downstream crate rather than imagining it.

  The library and the CLI stay one crate, so `cargo add oinkie` and `cargo install oinkie` both work under one name and a release is one upload rather than two that can half-succeed. What the CLI needs and the library does not — `env_logger`, `indicatif` and `rayon`, measured rather than assumed — is behind a `cli` feature that is on by default. `cargo add oinkie --no-default-features` builds 62 crates where the default builds 79; `regex` and the `crossbeam` family go with them.

  `clap` is not among them: `Ir` and `Algorithm` derive `ValueEnum`, so the library needs it too. It is the largest of the CLI's dependencies, which is why splitting the crate in two would not have bought much more than this.

  Nothing is published yet. `publish.yaml` gained a `crates-io` job, last in the graph because `cargo publish` cannot be undone, and it skips until `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` exists. The first upload is a decision rather than a side effect of merging.

- **A container image that is already the MCP server**, and one fewer name for the one that lifts.

  `quay.io/tama5/oinkie:mcp` is the light image with `mcp --root /work` as its default command, so a client's configuration ends at the image name. The binary is identical — `--features mcp` has always been passed once for every image — and so is the size, since it adds no layer.

  There is no Ghidra-plus-MCP image and there will not be one: the MCP server exposes no lift tool, so it would carry a gigabyte nothing in it can reach. `ghidra` is both the CLI and the server already.

  **The `full` tag is gone; use `ghidra`.** They have always been the same image under two names. A tag that stops being pushed does not disappear — it stays at the last version that had it — so `quay.io/tama5/oinkie:full` and `:0.5.0-full` should be deleted rather than left to look current.

- angr is no longer an advertised lifter. It was declared early, ahead of any work on it, and stayed a name in a list whose only reachable outcome was an error. It comes back when there is something behind it.

  Removing it also removed the only backend with no installation directory, so `home_spec` stops returning an `Option` and `find_home` loses the branch that said `--home` means nothing here. Neither could be reached once angr was the only case, and an unreachable error path is one nothing keeps honest.
- The install page names the JDK Ghidra actually needs. It said "typically JDK 17 or later"; Ghidra 12 refuses 17, and the repository's other two statements of the requirement — the lifter's README and the `full` container image — already said 21. Following the install page led to a failure whose message, `Unable to prompt user for JDK path, no TTY detected`, says nothing about versions at all, so the page now names that symptom too.
- The publication list in the README runs newest first, the way the site's Academic page already did, and both gain a submission to the International Journal of Software Innovation on how statically linked libraries distort cross-platform birthmark similarity.
